subject: Climate & Environment
title: Agriculture's Thirst
description: A fast breakdown of Agriculture's Thirst for builders.

hook.text: Agriculture uses 70% of all freshwater withdrawn worldwide. Industry and homes split the rest.

buildup.text: It takes 15,000 liters of water to produce one kilogram of beef.

discovery.text: Flood irrigation — the oldest method — wastes up to 50% of water through evaporation.

twist.text: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to roots and can cut usage by 60% with higher yields.

climax.text: Feeding 10 billion people by 2050 requires growing more food with less water — not more.

punchline.text: The world's biggest water user is the one that feeds us.

quiz.question: What share of global freshwater does agriculture use?

details.summary: Agriculture consumes roughly 70 percent of global freshwater withdrawals, mostly through irrigation. Inefficient flood irrigation wastes enormous volumes, while growing food demand from a rising population will require 50 percent more water by 2050 without major efficiency improvements.
details.whyItMatters: Feeding the world sustainably requires producing more food with less water. Agricultural water efficiency is the single largest lever for addressing global water scarcity.
takeaways: Agriculture uses about 70 percent of all freshwater withdrawals
Flood irrigation wastes significant volumes of water
Drip irrigation can cut water use by up to 50 percent

faq.question: What is the most water-efficient irrigation method?
faq.answer: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to plant roots through a network of tubes and emitters, using 30 to 50 percent less water than flood irrigation. It also reduces fertilizer runoff and can increase crop yields by maintaining optimal soil moisture consistently.

faq.question: Which crops use the most water?
faq.answer: Rice, cotton, sugarcane, and almonds are among the most water-intensive crops. Producing one kilogram of rice requires roughly 2,500 liters of water. Shifting dietary patterns and growing less water-intensive crops in arid regions could save enormous volumes.
